Hemophilia

Local PBM shortened post-extraction hemostasis time in one controlled cohort of people with hemophilia, and a mouse experiment reported faster wound closure. The clinical evidence remains limited to one non-randomized dental study and does not establish systemic disease control.

Evidence summary

What the evidence suggests

Local PBM may shorten post-extraction hemostasis time in people with hemophilia. Mouse and platelet findings support biological plausibility, but no trial has tested systemic bleeding control.

Summary of the Evidence

The evidence suggests that local PBM may shorten post-extraction hemostasis time in people with hemophilia and may support wound closure in a mouse model. The only human evidence is one non-randomized dental cohort, and no trial tests systemic disease control.

Human and clinical evidence

In the dental cohort, 30 participants received standard care plus low-level laser therapy at the extraction socket and 30 received standard care alone. Mean time to hemostasis was 22.42% shorter with PBM. Rebleeding occurred in 4 of 30 PBM participants and 13 of 30 controls, while postoperative factor replacement was used in 3 of 30 and 12 of 30, respectively. Because allocation was not randomized and outcomes were local to dental extraction, the findings do not show correction of the underlying clotting disorder (Kelkar et al. 2023).

Animal evidence

In hemophilic mice with 3-mm skin punch wounds, wounds closed by day 10 after laser treatment and by day 13 after sham treatment; wounds in non-hemophilic mice closed by day 9. This supports a local wound-healing effect in the model, not a systemic bleeding effect in people (Hoffman and Monroe 2012).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

The mouse publication also reported greater clot rigidity and platelet activity in human platelet-rich plasma after illumination. Isolated platelet experiments found increased mitochondrial membrane potential and greater binding of coagulation factors to activated platelets. These laboratory findings are methods within the same publication, not additional clinical studies.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The dental study’s abstract and database record do not report the wavelength, dose, or exposure schedule, so its protocol cannot be compared reliably with the mouse work. The mouse wounds received visible red light at 650 nm and 12 J/cm² on three successive days. No head-to-head or dose-finding test established an optimal exposure.

Interpretation

The clearest human finding is shorter local hemostasis time in one controlled cohort, accompanied by fewer rebleeding events and fewer postoperative factor-replacement treatments. These findings require randomized replication and do not establish systemic control of hemophilia.

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Post-extraction hemostasis: mean time to hemostasis was 22.42% shorter with PBM plus standard care than with standard care alone in a 60-person cohort.

Rebleeding occurred in 4/30 versus 13/30 participants, and postoperative factor replacement in 3/30 versus 12/30 (Kelkar et al. 2023).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low for reduced post-extraction hemostasis time.

Very low for systemic hemostasis or disease control.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

One prospective controlled cohort reported faster local hemostasis and fewer rebleeding and factor-replacement events, but allocation was not randomized and the finding has not been independently replicated. The mouse and platelet experiments add biological detail, not proof of patient benefit. No human study has tested systemic bleeding control (Kelkar et al. 2023; Hoffman and Monroe 2012).
